anchor: The wish, that of the living whole
title: In Memoriam LV: 'The wish, that of the living whole'
short: Section LV in standard numbering (titled LIV in this archive): the wish for immortality seems divine, but Nature appears indifferent to individual lives.
body: In Memoriam A. H. H. (published anonymously in 1850) mourns Arthur Henry Hallam, Tennyson's closest Cambridge friend and his sister Emily's fiancé, who died suddenly in Vienna on 15 September 1833. Its 131 sections and frame poems were written over some seventeen years. This is section LV in the standard numbering. Bradley's paraphrase: the wish that no life should fail beyond the grave seems a divine instinct, yet Nature is so careless of individual life that she gives it no support, and the poet can scarcely keep a dumb trust. 'The living whole' means all living things together.

anchor: The likest God within the soul
title: The likest God within the soul
short: The desire for immortality is taken as the most godlike thing in us, perhaps a trace of the divine image.
body: The first stanza is a question: does not the wish for universal survival come from what is most like God in the soul? The thought recalls the creation of humanity 'in the image of God' (Genesis 1:27), and suggests an argument from desire: so strong and unselfish a longing must have a divine origin. The question form leaves the argument hopeful but not secure.

sources.cite: Bible, King James Version, Genesis 1:27

anchor: Are God and Nature then at strife
title: Are God and Nature then at strife
short: The central question of LV-LVI: whether the God of love and the Nature revealed by science contradict each other.
body: Nature is personified as a female agent with 'evil dreams' and 'secret meaning'. The opposition of a loving God to an indifferent Nature was sharpened by the geology Tennyson read in 1837, notably Lyell's Principles of Geology, according to his son's Memoir. The Memoir also notes that the 'evolution' sections were read to friends some years before Chambers's Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation (1844).

anchor: So careful of the type she seems
title: So careful of the type ... So careless of the single life
short: Nature appears to preserve the species ('type') while being careless of the individual.
body: 'Type' means the species or kind. Bradley quotes Buffon's remark that nature cares little for individuals and concerns herself only with the species. The antithesis 'careful ... careless' balances the two lines on one root. Section LVI will take up the line and reject even this consolation, since fossils show species too are destroyed. The opposition between species and individual was a commonplace of eighteenth-century natural history before it became Darwinian. For a mourner the individual is everything, so Nature's preference is a direct wound.

sources.cite: A. C. Bradley, A Commentary on Tennyson's In Memoriam, 3rd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1910), note on sect. LV, ll. 7-8
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'type'

title: of fifty seeds / She often brings but one to bear
short: Nature's wastefulness: most seeds never germinate. Tennyson later said 'fifty' should be 'myriad'.
body: Bradley records Tennyson's own note that 'fifty' should have been 'myriad', though he never altered the text. The image of profuse seed and few survivors was a commonplace of natural history and political economy (Malthus's argument on population had made overproduction a familiar idea). It may also call up, ironically, the parable of the sower, where most seed falls on unfruitful ground (Matthew 13:3-8). Darwin later made such superabundance central to natural selection, after this poem was written.

anchor: I falter where I firmly trod
title: I falter where I firmly trod, / And falling
short: A spiritual stumble on the stairs of faith; Bradley compares the chorus's words to Antigone falling against Justice's throne.
body: Bradley compares Sophocles' Antigone (853-855), where the chorus tells Antigone that, going to the extreme of daring, she has stumbled against the high throne or step of Justice. Tennyson transfers the image to faith: the poet stumbles on stairs he once climbed securely. 'Weight of cares' explains the fall; doubt is felt as a burden. The movement from firm treading to faltering and falling is the section's turning point, from argument to helpless gesture.

sources.cite: A. C. Bradley, A Commentary on Tennyson's In Memoriam, 3rd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1910), note on sect. LV, ll. 14-15

title: the great world's altar-stairs / That slope thro' darkness up to God
short: The world as a vast temple whose stairs lead up through darkness to God, like Jacob's ladder.
body: The image makes creation a sanctuary and life an ascent toward an altar hidden in the dark. It recalls Jacob's ladder reaching to heaven (Genesis 28:12), and Bradley compares a passage in The Princess (VII) about scaling 'the shining steps of Nature' with man. Here, though, the steps slope 'thro' darkness': the way to God is real but unlit.

anchor: I stretch lame hands of faith
title: lame hands of faith
short: Faith pictured as crippled hands groping in the dark, unable to grasp.
body: 'Lame' transfers the weakness of legs to hands. The phrase may recall Hebrews 12:12, 'lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees', an exhortation to the faint-hearted. The verbs 'stretch', 'grope', 'gather', 'call' describe a blind man's search, the bodily form of doubt. Each verb is weaker than the last, so the syntax itself loses strength as the section approaches its faint close. The hands that once clasped Hallam's (section VII) now grope at nothing.

sources.cite: Bible, King James Version, Hebrews 12:12

title: gather dust and chaff
short: What reason picks up in its search is worthless: dust and husks instead of grain.
body: Bradley glosses the phrase as what the poet gets 'in trying to reason', and compares The Two Voices, 'a dust of systems and of creeds'. Chaff is the husk winnowed from grain and blown away, a biblical image of the worthless (Psalm 1:4). The reasoning mind finds no nourishment; only feeling, 'what I feel is Lord of all', remains. Section LVI will make Nature's own speech an answer to this faint trust.

sources.cite: A. C. Bradley, A Commentary on Tennyson's In Memoriam, 3rd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1910), note on sect. LV, l. 18
Bible, King James Version, Psalm 1:4

title: the larger hope
short: Tennyson's son explained it as the hope that the whole human race would finally be purified and saved.
body: Hallam Tennyson's Memoir (I.321) says the poet meant by 'the larger hope' that the whole human race would, perhaps through ages of suffering, be purified and saved, a hope wider than the orthodox doctrine of salvation for some and eternal punishment for others. The phrase became a watchword in Victorian debates over eternal punishment; Tennyson's friend F. D. Maurice lost his professorship at King's College London in 1853 partly over this question. Bradley wonders whether this is also the 'far-off divine event' of the Epilogue. The adverb 'faintly' keeps the trust weak.
